message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection directly from here, but I can walk you through a few quick ways to check your own speed on most systems.

---

## 1. Use an online speed‑test website  
The simplest method is to visit a reputable speed‑test site:

| Site | How to use |
|------|------------|
| **Speedtest.net** (by Ookla) | Go to <https://www.speedtest.net> and click “Go”. |
| **Fast.com** (by Netflix) | Visit <https://fast.com> – it starts automatically. |
| **Google Speed Test** | Search “internet speed test” in Google; the built‑in widget will appear. |

These sites give you download, upload, and ping (latency) results in a few seconds.

---

## 2. Run a command‑line test (cross‑platform)

If you prefer a terminal/command‑prompt approach, you can use the free **speedtest‑cli** tool.  
Below are instructions for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

### a. Install `speedtest-cli`

| OS | Install command |
|----|-----------------|
| **Windows** (PowerShell) | ```powershell -Command "pip install speedtest-cli"``` |
| **macOS / Linux** | ```bash -c "pip install speedtest-cli"``` |

> **Tip:** If you don’t have `pip` (Python’s package manager) installed, you’ll need to install Python first. On Windows you can get it from <https://www.python.org/downloads/>; on macOS it’s usually pre‑installed, and on Linux you can use your distro’s package manager (`sudo apt install python3-pip`, `sudo dnf install python3-pip`, etc.).

### b. Run the test

Once installed, just type:

```bash
speedtest
```

or, if you want a more concise output:

```bash
speedtest --simple
```

This will ping the nearest server, then report:

- **Download speed** (Mbps)
- **Upload speed** (Mbps)
- **Latency** (ms)

---

## 3. Quick test via PowerShell (Windows only)

If you’re on Windows and don’t want to install anything, you can use PowerShell’s built‑in `Invoke-WebRequest` to download a file and estimate speed. It’s a rough estimate, but it can give you a ballpark figure.

```powershell
$uri = "https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin"   # 100 MB test file
$start = Get-Date
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $uri -OutFile "$env:TEMP\speedtest.bin"
$end = Get-Date
$bytes = (Get-Item "$env:TEMP\speedtest.bin").Length
$seconds = ($end - $start).TotalSeconds
$mbps = ($bytes / 1MB) / $seconds
Write-Host "Approx. download speed: $([math]::Round($mbps,2)) Mbps"
Remove-Item "$env:TEMP\speedtest.bin"
```

> **Caution:** This downloads a 100 MB file, so use it only if you’re okay with that data usage.

---

## 4. Using `curl` (Linux/macOS)

If you have `curl` and `pv` (pipe viewer) installed, you can do a quick test:

```bash
curl -o /dev/null -w "%{speed_download}\n" https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin
```

This prints the average download speed in bytes per second.

---

### What to do next?

1. **Pick a method** that feels comfortable for you.  
2. **Run the test** and note the numbers.  
3. **Compare** them to the speed you’re supposed to get from your ISP.  

If you run into any trouble (e.g., “command not found”, “pip not installed”), let me know which OS you’re on and what error you see, and I can help troubleshoot!
